turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?
turns.patient_response: Well, I came in because... I just can't stop thinking about how the left side of my face looks. It just looks off to me. Like, my nose and my jaw, they look crooked. I see it in every ID photo, and whenever I have to turn my camera on for online classes, it's right there. People tell me they don't see it, but... I feel like everyone in the CNC lab is noticing it. Like they're looking at my crooked face before they even look at my work. It's just really getting to me.

symptom_reasoning.S067: The patient describes persistent preoccupation with perceived asymmetry and crookedness of their nose and jaw that others report they do not see.

turns.doctor_question: How much time per day would you say you spend thinking about or checking how your face looks?
turns.patient_response: It's hard to give an exact number of hours, but it takes up a huge part of my day. Mostly before I leave for school... I just get stuck. I'll be in the bathroom checking my face in the mirror, and then I use my phone camera to check it again. I spend a lot of time fixing my hair or changing my shirts to try and hide the angle. I even keep asking my mom if it looks weird. Sometimes I'm doing all this for so long that I actually miss my lab completely. Or if I do make it, I show up too wiped out to even focus on anything.

symptom_reasoning.S068: The patient describes engaging in extensive appearance-related repetitive behaviors, including mirror and phone camera checking, camouflaging with hair and clothing, and seeking reassurance from their mother.
